units.translation: and to tell of the winged (Hermann: winged) and the land-walking and the wind-swift (Blomfield: wind-swift, for wind-swift) goats' wrath,
having given an oath (thus from the scholium, for crossing) to speak nothing unjust.
judge, so that I may tell these things.
tell me now this all-wise name.
telling the shepherd of her toils.
he gave this oracle, to tell this Orestes never to pay honors to his mother.
you yourself, having learned these things, now tell me.
to tell these just powers from Zeus.
guide, one who shows the way
guide, one who shows the way
The scholiast explains it by τοὺς φράσαντας [those who have shown]. The word is not found elsewhere, except that the proper name Φράστωρ [Phrastor] exists.
send companions and guides of the local people.
Triclinius wrongly wrote φρατόρων [of the clansmen], ignorant of the old Attic form, about which I have spoken in Thes. vol. 8 p. 1036.
what lustral water of the clansmen will receive me?
(from the Doric form δαλέομαι [I destroy] of the verb δηλέομαι [I destroy]) harming or destroying the mind.
The scholiast explains it by παρακίνησις τῶν φρενών [disturbance of the mind]. In M a corrector wrote in the margin οἶμαι φρενοδαής [I think mind-burning].
such are the counsels and words of the frenzied that one may hear.
to bring to one's senses, to make wise, to admonish
to bring to one's senses, to make wise, to admonish
you are far better at admonishing others than yourself.
I will instruct no longer in riddles.
and you have admonished me not least.
madness brought together the frenzied bridal pair.
In the proper sense of the midriff, the plural is found
which the scholiast explains as ἀντὶ τοῦ παράφρων γίνεται ὑπὸ τοῦ φόβου [instead of 'he becomes deranged by fear'].

the reading is seriously corrupt, and its emendation is altogether uncertain: about which I have spoken s.v. θυμοφθόρος [soul-destroying] p. 160 a. Triclinius' conjecture τὴν θυμοβόρον λυποφρένα [the soul-devouring grief-mind] is most foolish. What I conjectured in Philologus vol. 18 p. 661, after removing the glosses, satisfies the sense: καινοῦ θυμοφθόρου ἄλγους [of new soul-destroying grief].
Thus Heath corrected for φρενί [to the mind].

Thus I corrected the corrupt reading in M, ἐλεδέμας [wretched?], and added what had fallen out, φρένας [the mind], about which I have spoken in the Preface to the fifth Leipzig edition p. XXXIV, comparing similar passages Pr. 181 ἐμὰς δὲ φρένας ἐρέθισε διάτορος φόβος [piercing fear stirred my mind] and Suppl. 379 ἀμηχανῶ δὲ καὶ φόβος μ᾿ ἔχει φρένας [I am at a loss and fear holds my mind], and the Homeric ἐμὲ δὲ (or τοὺς δὲ) χλωρὸν δέος ἥρει [pale fear seized me (or them)] Il. 7, 470 and Od. 11, 43. 633.
the verse being corrupt or interpolated. Sophocles said ἔσω φρενῶν [within the mind] Ph. 1325, Euripides φρενῶν ἔσω [within the mind] Med. 316.
where in M βροτῶν [of mortals], which Hermann corrected from the scholiast's note ἡ τῆς φρενὸς μοῖρα [the portion of the mind].
